title: Before Reading the Labels
passage:
During a school trip, Taku visited a small local museum. One room surprised him because several objects were displayed without explanation cards. There was an old wooden tool, a metal box, and a strange glass bottle. Students were asked to guess what the objects had been used for before reading any information. Taku first thought the activity was childish. He wanted the correct answers immediately. However, as his group looked closely, their guesses became more thoughtful. They examined scratches, handles, weight, and shape. One student suggested that the wooden tool had been used in farming because soil remained in a narrow crack. Another thought the metal box might have carried food because it had a tight lid. The museum guide listened without saying who was right. She asked the students to explain what evidence supported each idea. After ten minutes, the guide gave them the labels. Some guesses were correct, while others were not. The metal box, for example, had carried tools rather than food. Yet Taku noticed that the wrong guesses were still useful because they had forced the group to pay attention to details they would otherwise have ignored. In the next room, every object had a full label. This time, Taku caught himself reading the text before really looking at the objects. He understood why the first room had been designed differently. Information can help us understand what we see, but it can also cause us to stop observing for ourselves. At the end of the visit, students were asked to choose one object and write both an observation and an interpretation. Taku chose a worn school bag from many decades ago. His observation was that one side of the handle was smoother than the other. His interpretation was that the owner may have carried it in the same hand every day. He could not prove that idea, but he could separate what he saw from what he believed it might mean. The guide said this difference was important in museums, science, and even daily life. People often mix facts with explanations without noticing. Taku left the museum with fewer facts memorized than he had expected, but with a new habit: look first, describe carefully, and only then decide what the evidence might mean.

Back at school, Taku tried the same method with a photograph in a history textbook. Before reading the caption, he listed only what he could actually see: clothing, objects, positions, and expressions. Then he wrote possible explanations separately. When he finally read the caption, some ideas were supported and others were not. The exercise took longer than simply reading the answer, but it made him notice how quickly the mind builds stories from limited evidence. His teacher explained that careful thinkers do not avoid interpretation; they make the difference between observation and interpretation visible. Taku began using phrases such as the evidence shows and this may suggest. Those phrases reminded him that confidence should match the strength of the evidence available.
translation:
校外学習で拓が訪れた小さな郷土博物館には、説明札が付いていない展示室がありました。古い木製道具、金属箱、不思議なガラス瓶などを見て、説明を読む前に用途を推測する活動です。最初、拓は子どもっぽいと思い、すぐ正解を知りたがりました。しかし観察を続けるうち、班の推測は具体的になりました。傷、持ち手、重さ、形を調べ、木の道具の隙間に土が残っているから農作業用ではないか、金属箱はふたが密閉できるから食べ物を運んだのではないか、などと考えました。案内人は正誤を言わず、『どんな証拠があるか』を説明させました。後で説明札を見ると、正しい推測も間違いもあり、金属箱は食べ物ではなく工具を入れる物でした。それでも拓は、間違った推測にも意味があったと気づきます。答えを先に読んでいたら見逃していた細部を観察できたからです。次の部屋ではすべてに詳しい説明があり、拓は物そのものを見る前に文章を読んでいる自分に気づきました。情報は理解を助ける一方、自分で観察することを止めさせる場合もあります。最後に、生徒は一つの展示物について『観察した事実』と『そこからの解釈』を別々に書きました。拓は古い学生かばんを選び、持ち手の片側だけが滑らかなことを事実として、持ち主が毎日同じ手で持ったのかもしれないと解釈しました。証明はできませんが、見たものと意味づけを分けることができます。案内人は、この区別は博物館だけでなく科学や日常生活でも大切だと話しました。拓は大量の知識より、『まず見て、丁寧に記述し、その後で意味を考える』という新しい習慣を持ち帰りました。

学校に戻った拓は、歴史教科書の写真でも同じ方法を試しました。説明文を読む前に服装、物、位置、表情など見える事実だけを書き、その後で解釈を分けて記しました。説明を確認すると、当たった推測も外れた推測もありました。先生は、考えることを避けるのではなく、観察と解釈の違いを見えるようにすることが大切だと説明しました。拓は『証拠が示す』『〜かもしれない』という表現を使い、証拠の強さに合った確信度を意識するようになりました。
